PARK CAPTURE

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
We are going to take the story forward and not just recap, we are trying to get to the bottom of why by questioning everything. We have an interview secured with Sizakela from JPC.

Summary:
[OPENING ACT – VISUAL INTRO]
Visual: Sweeping drone shot over Marks Park—lush fields, joggers, kids on swings, dogs chasing frisbees. Cut to the City of Joburg skyline creeping into frame.
(Presenter VO): “Lease rationalisation.” “Non-core assets.” And the word that says it all—“alienation.” They sound like routine municipal processes. But in Johannesburg, they’re being used to describe something far more contentious: a proposal that could see iconic green spaces—our city’s lungs—under threat.
Visuals: We need to have a montage here are visuals from the story of coming up – maybe from confront/juxtapose with protest/angry residents
(Jonker): “These aren’t just empty plots — they’re vital public spaces the City now wants to dispose of, rezone, and sell off. It’s a land grab.”
Visual: Map graphic – highlighting RE/33 Braamfontein 53 IR with overlays of areas like Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Botanical Gardens, Froggy Pond, Westdene Dam.
(Presenter VO): What’s at stake? This—173 hectares of public land that includes some of Joburg’s most treasured parks and recreation zones. It’s not “just the sports clubs” as the City claims—it’s an entire green corridor that could change forever.
[STORY FRAME – SETTING THE STAKES]
(Presenter Link): The City insists it’s just policy. But to residents, it feels like a land grab. And behind the bureaucratic jargon lies a simple question: if this was really just about updating leases — why not just renew them? Why launch an entirely new process that opens the door to rezoning, reclassification, and even permanent disposal? That’s what we set out to uncover.
Visual: Insert of JPC’s Sizeka Tshabalala from Facebook, then overlay headlines: "SIU finds Helen Botes guilty", "JPC in HAWKS crosshairs", "Joburg residents in uproar over parks".
(Presenter VO): PREVIOUS STORY RECAP The Johannesburg Property Company—tasked with leading this controversial land review—says it’s working to rebuild public trust. But its credibility is in tatters.
Last year Carte Blanche reported on how its former CEO, Helen Botes, was found guilty of financial misconduct in a Special Investigating Unit probe into COVID-era cleaning tenders—yet she was kept on.
Now, formal charges have been filed, and the HAWKS are investigating a lease deal involving Proton House—an inner-city property allegedly handed to politically connected interests under questionable terms.
(Presenter Link): The JPC says it’s cleaning house, but keeping Helen Botes in the fold has raised eyebrows—and so has their strategy to earn back the public’s trust. By targeting parks and sports grounds in a bid to boost revenue, are they not alienating the very communities they’re meant to serve?
(Presenter VO): Johannesburg Property Company General Manager, Sizakela Tshabalala, has been everywhere—on radio, in print, online—reassuring residents this isn’t a land grab, but a cleanup.
Upsound – Facebook video: “Some people are still paying R2 or R49 a year on leases that were signed more than 30 years ago. It’s not sustainable.”
“We’re not taking anything away. We’re just trying to modernise, to make it fair.”
(Presenter VO): She insists it’s just about bringing outdated leases in line with today’s market. But residents aren’t convinced. Is this really about revenue—or is there a deeper, politically driven agenda at play?
Visual: Park/sports visuals throughout entire piece to illustrate what they’re used for.

[ACT 1 – THE ALARM IS RAISED]
Visual: Cut to Cllr Nicolene Jonker at her desk, flipping through the Council agenda.
(Presenter VO): It was buried in the paperwork. A dry-sounding council item about lease reviews. But when DA councillor Nicolene Jonker looked closer, one phrase jumped off the page: Municipal Asset Transfer Regulations.
(Jonker): “This isn’t about updating leases. This is a formal alienation process—the first legal step toward disposal.”
Visual: Council document highlighting ATR references. Zoom in on phrases like “alienation,” “surplus land,” and “public participation.”
(Presenter VO): And that matters. Because the Asset Transfer References are only triggered when a municipality intends to sell or transfer public land. Not when it's simply renewing a lease.
Visual: Community protests. Residents holding placards: “HANDS OFF OUR PARKS!” “MARKS PARK IS OURS!”
Visual: Cut to the comedic AI-generated protest song.
(Presenter VO): Just bringing up this issue sparks outrage in the community. It’s struck such a nerve, even the protests have gone musical. A viral AI-generated anthem did what formal petitions couldn’t—put Joburg on notice. So let’s take a look at the land in question.
Visuals: MAP again
(Presenter VO): The area flagged in JPC’s own documents spans up to 173 hectares—a sweeping green belt that includes Pirates Club, Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Melville Koppies, and parts of the Botanical Gardens.
Land is a sensitive subject, but also a political bargaining chip. Now, political parties are jumping on the bandwagon—framing green spaces as a luxury. Some argue these areas could be better used for low-cost housing, rather than recreation.
In a city like Johannesburg, green spaces aren’t luxuries—they’re lifelines. Parks and sports grounds are protected public assets, meant to serve communities, not be quietly sold off.
(Jonker): The leases could be undervalued, but currently its normal for them to be only R500 a month, not millions. And the current lease holders take care of the properties paying the water/elec/lights, mowing the lawns, so they have value.
(Presenter VO): In interviews Tshabalala has said these properties like Marks Park could be worth R10 million.
00:04:00–00:04:22 “So if you look at Marks Park and the fact that when we enter into a lease … considering the value of that property … the lease, if we are looking at its market value today, we anticipate that the rental that we need to get as the city is in excess of R10 million.”
(Presenter VO): But could they know that if there’s been no feasibility study done?
(Jonker): They’re doing this backwards, you first do the feasibility study, then you do the public participation process, and you give more information about the land. Currently we know nothing.
(Presenter VO): And what Sizeka doesn’t say—is that the lease for Marks Park is a notarial one, registered in 1994, valid until 2043. Legally binding. And already limited to sport and recreation.
[Examples of where JPC has failed]
(Presenter VO): And why should residents trust the Johannesburg Property Company? Its track record is riddled with poor management. Just look at James and Ethel Gray Park—where paddle courts appeared overnight.
Jonker (upsound): “Why would you allow these to pop up—and then have no benefit to the City?”
(Presenter VO): Was it simple oversight that none of that revenue goes back to the City? And what about Bryanston Sports Club—did residents somehow miss the public participation signs?
Jonker (upsound): “They were stuck at the back of the room, facing the wall. No one saw them. Public participation feels like a box-ticking exercise.”
(Presenter VO): Now, that sports club is under review. Its future? Completely up to the City. And that’s exactly what’s raising concern.
CASE STUDY: PIRATES RUGBY CLUB
Cut to: Pirates Rugby Club, where the local manager describes years of community investment, public use, and rising anxiety.
Pirates owner: “We run this space for the people. We pay for water, electricity, maintenance—and we’re the ones being targeted?”
Visuals: Maybe some humour with presenter – take a breather park visuals.
(Presenter VO): On 702 radio, Sizeka Tshabalala says the review isn’t about selling parks, but about unlocking more sports and community opportunities.
(approx. 8:52–10:49):
“We’re simply looking at how to diversify usage — can we introduce additional sports codes, make these facilities more active and community-focused?”
... We are saying that if there are football grounds, what other sports can we bring into that facility to make it more active?”
(Presenter VO): But is that really the job of a property management company? Shouldn’t they be managing assets—not deciding what sports should be played? And if this is really about revenue, why aren’t they looking for money elsewhere?
Pause visuals…

[ACT 2 – THE MONEY AND WHO DO YOU TRUST?]
Visual: Split-screen — on one side, JPC statements. On the other, maps showing affected areas—up to 173 hectares. Cut to aerials of Melville Koppies and Emmarentia Dam.
(Presenter VO): And yet, nowhere in the JPC’s own business plan is “disposal of public green space” mentioned. (show business plan visuals)
Graphic: City-owned derelict buildings. Hijacked inner-city properties. Overlay: “Why not start here?”
(Presenter VO): If the City really wanted to boost revenue, why not start with hijacked buildings? Why not recover millions in unpaid advertising fees or charge city departments for building maintenance?
(Jonker:) “If the City was serious about revenue, it wouldn’t be coming after parks. It would be going after hijacked buildings, collecting what’s owed in advertising revenue, its collected none of that this year! You know they maintain the Joburg city department buildings, they could be billing its own departments for maintenance.”
Presenter VO: So come back to the question: why?
Presenter Link (on camera, walking through park): We’ve asked a lot of people, some say the City’s budget is under pressure—and instead of fixing its own broken revenue systems, it’s going after the low-hanging fruit: functional parks and sports clubs that already work. With the 2026 local elections approaching, could green spaces be eyed for future low-cost housing?
(Presenter VO): On radio, Tshabalala insists that the idea of building housing hasn’t even crossed their minds.
Tshabalala Tshabalala on radio interview. “We have not even considered — it has not come to our mind — that there can be potential for a block of flats or residential for that matter. For now, we are looking at the facility in terms of its right, which is looking purely at sports.”
(Presenter LINK) [Walking Into Frame – Confront Setup]: Tshabalala says it’s all above board—just about updating old leases. But with the scale of land involved, the laws used, and little transparency, residents are asking: is that really the full story?
(Presenter VO): We sat down with Tshabalala to find out.
[THE CITY RESPONDS in act 2]
LEGALITY & PROCESS
You’ve said there’s a notarial lease in place until 2044 for Marks Park—so on what legal basis are you trying to override it now? Isn’t that lease binding?
If this is really just a lease review, then why not simply renew the leases? Why invoke the Asset Transfer Regulations—meant for disposing of public land?
Why is public participation only happening after Council approval? The law says it must come first—aren’t you in breach of that?
TRANSPARENCY & TRUST
Why hasn’t the public been told that up to 173 hectares of green space could be affected?
At James and Ethel Gray, padel courts popped up with no participation process—and none of that revenue comes back to the City. Why?
What participation process was there at Bryanston Sports Club? Posters were hidden. You see, this is why people don’t trust JPC.
FINANCIAL LOGIC
You’ve claimed Marks Park could generate R10 million in rent. Based on what? Has a feasibility study been done?
These clubs already pay for water, electricity, security, and rates—what exactly is the City contributing in return?
Wouldn’t it make more financial sense to recover the millions owed by other City departments to JPC for building maintenance—rather than threaten functional green spaces?
Why target well-used parks and clubs when hijacked buildings and rundown city properties lie neglected? Why not start there?
JPC’S ROLE & OVERREACH
Why is the Johannesburg Property Company deciding which sports are “relevant” enough to keep? Isn’t that the mandate of the Sports Department?
Where in the City’s business or asset management plan does it say that parks, sports fields, and cemeteries are up for disposal?

[FINAL 3 – WHAT’S AT STAKE]
(Presenter Link): In principle, most of us agree—land and housing for the poor are essential. But is it any wonder that when proposals like this come from the City, they’re met with deep scepticism? This is the same administration that once promised a “Mega City”… and was later exposed for looting COVID relief funds. Now suddenly, it’s about building homes for the poor? The public’s cynicism isn’t unfounded.
Visual: Families in the park. Tai chi in the grass. Soccer games. Laughter.
(Presenter VO): If Marks Park falls, what’s next? Melville Koppies? The Botanical Gardens?
Jonker: “These spaces aren’t luxuries. They’re constitutional rights. And once they’re gone—we never get them back. You need them to actually put up high rise flats, its part of the city cy-laws to have green spaces”
(Presenter link): The City says this is about financial value. But green spaces offer something far more valuable: breathing room, community, connection.
(Presenter VO): And before we give that up—we need to ask: who benefits from this? And what will be left for the rest of us?
OUTRO – Fade to black. Park aerial fades into city skyline.
END.



Further information:
Visual Note for Script – Director’s Brief
We’re aiming for bold, cinematic visuals to anchor this story and give it scale. That means sweeping drone footage of the Johannesburg skyline, contrasted with expansive overhead shots of the green spaces under review—Marks Park, the Botanical Gardens, Melville Koppies, etc. We’ll also need low-angle shots of key city buildings, especially the JPC offices, to visually represent institutional power.
Throughout the piece, we’ll cut to “breathing space” moments—scenes of people using the parks. These should feel warm, organic, and grounded: children playing, families relaxing, joggers, dog walkers, informal soccer games. We want the audience to see what's at stake. (We’ll need to get permissions from City Parks to film these areas—potentially with a fee—and I’ll handle those requests.)
Framing & Tone:
This story has been in the news, so we’re not here to rehash it. We’re here to deepen the conversation and push it forward. That means sharp, informed questioning, paired with a clear and compelling visual narrative.
The opening act runs a bit longer—around three minutes—because we need to recap our previous story, introduce the map and the core issue, and establish the key characters driving the narrative.
We’ll use Sizakela’s previous public statements (including her radio and Facebook clips) to set up the confrontation efficiently and focus on getting real answers—not soundbites. This is a deliberate decision: keep the confrontation short but meaningful, with layered build-up across the acts.
We’ve planted clues throughout the script:
In Act 1, we raise early questions about the lease process and hint at the politicking, with political parties calling parks a "luxury."
In Act 2, before the confrontation, we introduce deeper suspicions—suggesting these parks may be seen as cash cows or tools to manipulate ward demographics ahead of 2026.
Then we go straight into the confrontation—direct, clear, and urgent.
Presenter Direction:
The presenter must be part of the story. They should be seen walking through the parks, interacting with residents, asking questions aloud, and reacting with genuine curiosity or concern. Their presence anchors the viewer and helps humanise a potentially dry, bureaucratic issue.
Tone & Engagement:
We’re not doing a long list of case studies—this isn’t a legal brief. We’re taking viewers to Pirates Rugby Club because it’s vibrant and relatable, something our audience will enjoy. We’ll also inject some levity with the AI protest song, and hopefully include community protest visuals if they happen.
This is a story about green spaces—but also about power, trust, and the city’s future. So it needs to be sharp, visually rich, and people-focused. Every scene must remind the audience what we’re really fighting to protect.

Script:


Shots of other municipalities… and then going into Joburg to widen scope of story…
(Moleli VO): Across the country, cash‑strapped municipalities are scrambling to raise money — and Johannesburg seems to have its eye on public spaces - from parks to sports fields.
Visual: Drones of these spaces in joburg…
(Moleli VO): The City boasts that Joburg is the world’s largest manmade urban forest — but it doesn’t have a formal register of its green spaces. Many are leased to clubs and community groups that maintain and use them.
Visual: Close up shots of people using these spaces
(Pat Carolin): We are providing a service to the people, now the city is trying to make a decision on what to do with the asset that actually belongs to those people.
(Moleli VO): The City has announced the leases of 91 parks and green spaces are being reviewed.
And residents fear the real plan is to redevelop or even sell off their beloved parks.
(Farouk Khan): We're definitely scared because, obviously, our fate is in the hands of the city council as such.
(Moleli VO) Outraged residents are responding as only South Africans can.
Visual: protest song clip
[TRANSITION]

[ACT 1 – THE ALARM IS RAISED]
Visual: Cllr Nicolene Jonker at her desk, flipping through the Council agenda.
(Moleli VO): Jo’burg councillor Nicolene Jonker was reading through obscure council paperwork when a familiar property caught her eye.
(Jonker): To my horror, I saw the name Marks Park. It’s the city’s pride and joy.
(Moleli VO): Mark’s Park is a Joburg landmark and home to a range of sports facilities. She’d spotted its name in a report by the Johannesburg Property Company, or JPC, which manages the City’s property portfolio.
(Moleli): What made you think something is fishy here?
(Jonker): Well, it's speaking about a non-core asset, a non utilised space. And another thing that really stood out was the alienation.
(Moleli VO): Oddly, the report described it as a “non‑core asset” and the word “alienation” in property law means there was a planned transfer of ownership through a sale or lease.
(Moleli VO): The City’s green space leases typically run for 25 years. Marks Park’s lease was renewed in 2018, and still has 19 years to go. So why announce a review now? According to officials, the property is paying too little.
(Tshabalala Facebook video): “If you look at Marks Park, this city is receiving R49 per annum — you can see that doesn’t make any business sense.”
(Moleli VO): JPC General Manager Sizeka Tshabalala has told the media the aim is simply to update rentals to match current market values.


(Tshabalala): “We anticipate that the rental that we need to get as the city is in excess of R10 million.”
(Moleli VO): That’s R10 million for just one property! A substantial jump from what’s currently being paid. The local community believes something much more dubious is behind the move.
(Jonker): But this particular item said sale.
(Moleli VO): The JPC report appeared to suggest that a 173‑hectare green corridor in the suburb of Emmarentia could be put up for sale.
It includes not only Marks Park, but also the Melville Koppies and Botanical Gardens — land donated to the City in the 1930s, on condition it remains public and its biodiversity protected. (show MAP)

Moleli: The JPC has suggested sites like Marks Park and various other green spaces could bring in millions for the city?
Jonker: I do think it's prime land and they can probably sell it for a lot. But let's be open, honest and tell the residents what you really want to do.
(Moleli VO): Carte Blanche and other media have in the past reported on irregular tenders and other allegations linked to senior JPC officials. As a result, public trust in the organisation is low.
(Moleli link): The JPC claims it’s cleaning house. But targeting parks and sports grounds to boost revenue, isn’t it driving away the very communities they’re trying to win back?
PAUSE
(Moleli VO): The parks saga comes amid a significant budget crisis in our economic hub. Simply put, the City is running out of money.
In the last financial year, it posted a R300 million deficit, so could it be that the City is now eyeing public assets for revenue?
Pat Carolin manages the Bryanston Sport Club and says they're anything but lucrative.
(Pat Carolin): We're a municipal non-profit club open to the public, and we run at a small loss of about R150,000. Last financial year, we spent R1.3 million just on the maintenance of these grounds. If we were to pay market-related rentals, we wouldn't then be able to afford the maintenance on their asset.
(Moleli VO): The club’s lease was up for review late last year. But, oddly, a report on the matter quietly slipped through council - without Bryanston’s management team knowing.
Pause: Mac and Carolin playing Tennis - DRONE and closeup visuals
Changing the lease on properties valued above R10 million - like Marks Park and the Bryanston Sports Club - requires public participation. But, by June, Bryanston had missed the opportunity to object.
(Pat Carolin): They didn't notify any of the local newspapers. Even the delivery of the notice to us was shrouded in a bit of secrecy. We found it lying on the floor outside. This notice wasn’t dated.
Pause: Go to Emmarentia Dam sequence with Mac
(Moleli VO): Marks Park and Bryanston Sports Club are among 91 public spaces under review. Each has its own report, with the City looking to charge what the properties are worth.
(Moleli link): So, here’s the problem, no one outside of council has actually seen the report. And until it’s made public, no one really knows what it says.

(Moleli VO): But we did find evidence for Jonker’s claim that the City plans to sell parks, not JUST renegotiate the leases. It’s in a tender document explicitly listing Marks Park for sale.
PAUSE….

[ACT 2 – THE MONEY AND WHO DO YOU TRUST?]
(Moleli Link): So, are residents right to be worried about this land — or is it, as the JPC insists, just business as usual? We're here to cut through the noise and hear exactly what the JPC has to say.
Drone JPC
(Moleli VO): The JPC’s Sizeka Tshabalala says this is all a simple misunderstanding. But, from the outset, appears confused about the very origin of Mark’s Park.
(Moleli): Was this land donated to the city?
(Tshabalala): No, no it was purchased by the city in and around 1943.

(Moleli VO): We asked, but the City didn’t show us the purchase agreement, citing privacy.
MAP
Tshabalala clarified that the City isn’t reviewing leases on the entire 173 hectare green belt: only Marks Park. NOT the Koppies or Botanical Gardens. She says the current Marks Park lease is invalid because there was no public participation when it was renewed in 2018.
(Tshabalala): Before any lease can be concluded, there's always a council approval or a resolution. And there must also be a notice. We don't have a record of that.
(Moleli): Can it truly generate up to R10 million in rental?
(Tshabalala): I think it can, because when we get evaluation, it is from a professional, so if we are leasing it for 25 years, the valuation report advises us, over that period, you can generate this much.
(Moleli): You are not selling this land?
(Tshabalala): We are still going to continue leasing it for the same exact usage which is sports and recreation.
(Moleli VO): If that’s the case, why does the word “sale” appear on the council report - and on a tender document we uncovered?
Visual: Moleli shows her the document with sale on it.
(Moleli): So, I've got a document here. “Public participation for proposed sale”. Surely when people see this they will be worried, because this is obviously your document. City of Joburg, Property Company, in terms of the tender that went out.
(Tshabalala): Okay. No, no, no. It is not for a sale.
(Moleli): So, is this wrong?
(Tshabalala): Yes, it’s wrong. We have amended it.
(Moleli): When was it amended?
(Tshabalala): It has been amended right now.

(Moleli VO): But it’s not the first time this “mistake” has happened. The same “sale” slip up was repeated in the documents referring to Bryanston Sports Club.
(Tshabalala): We’re issuing an erratum, because it made reference to a sale instead of a lease.
(Moleli): Who keeps on making this mistake of a sale? Who writes these tender documents?
(Tshabalala): We compile a list of what needs to be done and we appoint service providers.
(Moleli): For Marks Park and now for Bryanston you're saying the same mistake was made.
(Tshabalala): It’s an erratum, yes.
(Moleli VO): But, sale or lease, it’s hard to avoid a glaring irony: The City wants to void the Mark’s Park lease because of a lack of public participation when it was renewed, and yet it apparently failed to conduct a public participation at Bryanston.
(Moleli): Were any local papers contacted?
(Tshabalala): Right now that's the process that we are following.

(Moleli link): So even if we accept that the word ‘sale’ was just a mistake and they meant ‘lease’ ... Either way, the money doesn’t go to the JPC. It goes directly to the city. and given their track record, that’s a concern.

[PAUSE]

[FINAL ACT 3 – WHAT’S AT STAKE]
Visuals of COUNCIL MEETING - Moleli comes to council chambers and watches…
(Moleli VO): Tshabalala promised the controversial JPC report would go before council for a vote the following day, but that didn’t happen.
(Joburg Councilor): We would like on behalf of the executive to withdraw… item 42
(Moleli link)(no tracksuit): It’s no surprise that after our interview with the JPC, item 42, which was meant to discuss the sale or lease of marks park was suddenly removed from the agenda…
(Jonker): It shows me that they've listened. They've listened to you, as Carte Blanche. but it's not off the table.

(Moleli VO): The JPC later confirmed it withdrew the report due to “factual” errors.

(Jonker:) To write out sale versus lease, it's totally different keys to type.


(Moleli link)(no tracksuit): Conversations about land use are important, but can you really blame the public for being little bit sceptical? This is the very department that was exposed for looting covid relief funds, and now they’re saying it's about the public benefiting from green spaces? Come on!

END.
OUTRO: The city says they withdrew
TEASER FOR CAP ON TUESDAY WP_FX3_2062 01:00: A CITY PROPOSAL, THREE SUSPICIOUS TYPING ERRORS AND LAND THAT COULD BE SOLD OR LEASED - ALL IN THE NAME OF PUBLIC BENEFIT, BUT WITH THE CITY’S HISTORY OF MISMANAGEMENT AND BROKEN PROMISES, RESIDENTS ARE NOT BUYING THE OFFICIAL STORY.

PROMO 1 X 21 seconds:
VO: From botanical gardens to rugby fields… the city says it’s just reviewing leases. But residents fear a land grab is already underway.
Upsound: Farouk Khan: We're definitely scared because, obviously, our fate is in the hands of the city council

VO: What’s really behind the City’s park review?

PROMO 2: “Follow the Money”
Jonker: If I didn’t make this big who-ha nobody would have known.
Upsound: (Pat Carolin): We are providing a service to the people, now the city is trying to make a decision on what to do with the asset that actually belongs to those people.
VO: Is the City targeting public green spaces as a way to cash in?

PROMO 3: “Face to Face” (Confrontation Tease)
VO: Are public green spaces up for sale or for lease renewal?
(Tshabalala) No, no, no. It is not for a sale.

text: Add New Proposal Shows Add New Show View All Shows 17 May 2026 - Carte Blanche HD 10 May 2026 - Carte Blanche HD 03 May 2026 - Carte Blanche HD 26 April 2026 - Carte Blanche HD 19 April 2026 - Carte Blanche HD 12 April 2026 - Carte Blanche HD 05 April 2026 - Carte Blanche HD Hi Lezanne [My Account] [Logout] Home Viewer Submissions Reports Contacts Music Cue Sheet Manage Users View Insert Edit Insert Insert Workflow PARK CAPTURE By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission Proposal Show: Carte Blanche Unique Selling Point: We are going to take the story forward and not just recap, we are trying to get to the bottom of why by questioning everything. We have an interview secured with Sizakela from JPC. Summary: [OPENING ACT – VISUAL INTRO] Visual: Sweeping drone shot over Marks Park—lush fields, joggers, kids on swings, dogs chasing frisbees. Cut to the City of Joburg skyline creeping into frame. (Presenter VO): “Lease rationalisation.” “Non-core assets.” And the word that says it all—“alienation.” They sound like routine municipal processes. But in Johannesburg, they’re being used to describe something far more contentious: a proposal that could see iconic green spaces—our city’s lungs—under threat. Visuals: We need to have a montage here are visuals from the story of coming up – maybe from confront/juxtapose with protest/angry residents (Jonker): “These aren’t just empty plots — they’re vital public spaces the City now wants to dispose of, rezone, and sell off. It’s a land grab.” Visual: Map graphic – highlighting RE/33 Braamfontein 53 IR with overlays of areas like Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Botanical Gardens, Froggy Pond, Westdene Dam. (Presenter VO): What’s at stake? This—173 hectares of public land that includes some of Joburg’s most treasured parks and recreation zones. It’s not “just the sports clubs” as the City claims—it’s an entire green corridor that could change forever. [STORY FRAME – SETTING THE STAKES] (Presenter Link): The City insists it’s just policy. But to residents, it feels like a land grab. And behind the bureaucratic jargon lies a simple question: if this was really just about updating leases — why not just renew them? Why launch an entirely new process that opens the door to rezoning, reclassification, and even permanent disposal? That’s what we set out to uncover. Visual: Insert of JPC’s Sizeka Tshabalala from Facebook, then overlay headlines: "SIU finds Helen Botes guilty", "JPC in HAWKS crosshairs", "Joburg residents in uproar over parks". (Presenter VO): PREVIOUS STORY RECAP The Johannesburg Property Company—tasked with leading this controversial land review—says it’s working to rebuild public trust. But its credibility is in tatters. Last year Carte Blanche reported on how its former CEO, Helen Botes, was found guilty of financial misconduct in a Special Investigating Unit probe into COVID-era cleaning tenders—yet she was kept on. Now, formal charges have been filed, and the HAWKS are investigating a lease deal involving Proton House—an inner-city property allegedly handed to politically connected interests under questionable terms. (Presenter Link): The JPC says it’s cleaning house, but keeping Helen Botes in the fold has raised eyebrows—and so has their strategy to earn back the public’s trust. By targeting parks and sports grounds in a bid to boost revenue, are they not alienating the very communities they’re meant to serve? (Presenter VO): Johannesburg Property Company General Manager, Sizakela Tshabalala, has been everywhere—on radio, in print, online—reassuring residents this isn’t a land grab, but a cleanup. Upsound – Facebook video: “Some people are still paying R2 or R49 a year on leases that were signed more than 30 years ago. It’s not sustainable.” “We’re not taking anything away. We’re just trying to modernise, to make it fair.” (Presenter VO): She insists it’s just about bringing outdated leases in line with today’s market. But residents aren’t convinced. Is this really about revenue—or is there a deeper, politically driven agenda at play? Visual: Park/sports visuals throughout entire piece to illustrate what they’re used for. [ACT 1 – THE ALARM IS RAISED] Visual: Cut to Cllr Nicolene Jonker at her desk, flipping through the Council agenda. (Presenter VO): It was buried in the paperwork. A dry-sounding council item about lease reviews. But when DA councillor Nicolene Jonker looked closer, one phrase jumped off the page: Municipal Asset Transfer Regulations. (Jonker): “This isn’t about updating leases. This is a formal alienation process—the first legal step toward disposal.” Visual: Council document highlighting ATR references. Zoom in on phrases like “alienation,” “surplus land,” and “public participation.” (Presenter VO): And that matters. Because the Asset Transfer References are only triggered when a municipality intends to sell or transfer public land. Not when it's simply renewing a lease. Visual: Community protests. Residents holding placards: “HANDS OFF OUR PARKS!” “MARKS PARK IS OURS!” Visual: Cut to the comedic AI-generated protest song. (Presenter VO): Just bringing up this issue sparks outrage in the community. It’s struck such a nerve, even the protests have gone musical. A viral AI-generated anthem did what formal petitions couldn’t—put Joburg on notice. So let’s take a look at the land in question. Visuals: MAP again (Presenter VO): The area flagged in JPC’s own documents spans up to 173 hectares—a sweeping green belt that includes Pirates Club, Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Melville Koppies, and parts of the Botanical Gardens. Land is a sensitive subject, but also a political bargaining chip. Now, political parties are jumping on the bandwagon—framing green spaces as a luxury. Some argue these areas could be better used for low-cost housing, rather than recreation. In a city like Johannesburg, green spaces aren’t luxuries—they’re lifelines. Parks and sports grounds are protected public assets, meant to serve communities, not be quietly sold off. (Jonker): The leases could be undervalued, but currently its normal for them to be only R500 a month, not millions. And the current lease holders take care of the properties paying the water/elec/lights, mowing the lawns, so they have value. (Presenter VO): In interviews Tshabalala has said these properties like Marks Park could be worth R10 million. 00:04:00–00:04:22 “So if you look at Marks Park and the fact that when we enter into a lease … considering the value of that property … the lease, if we are looking at its market value today, we anticipate that the rental that we need to get as the city is in excess of R10 million.” (Presenter VO): But could they know that if there’s been no feasibility study done? (Jonker): They’re doing this backwards, you first do the feasibility study, then you do the public participation process, and you give more information about the land. Currently we know nothing. (Presenter VO): And what Sizeka doesn’t say—is that the lease for Marks Park is a notarial one, registered in 1994, valid until 2043. Legally binding. And already limited to sport and recreation. [Examples of where JPC has failed] (Presenter VO): And why should residents trust the Johannesburg Property Company? Its track record is riddled with poor management. Just look at James and Ethel Gray Park—where paddle courts appeared overnight. Jonker (upsound): “Why would you allow these to pop up—and then have no benefit to the City?” (Presenter VO): Was it simple oversight that none of that revenue goes back to the City? And what about Bryanston Sports Club—did residents somehow miss the public participation signs? Jonker (upsound): “They were stuck at the back of the room, facing the wall. No one saw them. Public participation feels like a box-ticking exercise.” (Presenter VO): Now, that sports club is under review. Its future? Completely up to the City. And that’s exactly what’s raising concern. CASE STUDY: PIRATES RUGBY CLUB Cut to: Pirates Rugby Club, where the local manager describes years of community investment, public use, and rising anxiety. Pirates owner: “We run this space for the people. We pay for water, electricity, maintenance—and we’re the ones being targeted?” Visuals: Maybe some humour with presenter – take a breather park visuals. (Presenter VO): On 702 radio, Sizeka Tshabalala says the review isn’t about selling parks, but about unlocking more sports and community opportunities. (approx. 8:52–10:49): “We’re simply looking at how to diversify usage — can we introduce additional sports codes, make these facilities more active and community-focused?” ... We are saying that if there are football grounds, what other sports can we bring into that facility to make it more active?” (Presenter VO): But is that really the job of a property management company? Shouldn’t they be managing assets—not deciding what sports should be played? And if this is really about revenue, why aren’t they looking for money elsewhere? Pause visuals… [ACT 2 – THE MONEY AND WHO DO YOU TRUST?] Visual: Split-screen — on one side, JPC statements. On the other, maps showing affected areas—up to 173 hectares. Cut to aerials of Melville Koppies and Emmarentia Dam. (Presenter VO): And yet, nowhere in the JPC’s own business plan is “disposal of public green space” mentioned. (show business plan visuals) Graphic: City-owned derelict buildings. Hijacked inner-city properties. Overlay: “Why not start here?” (Presenter VO): If the City really wanted to boost revenue, why not start with hijacked buildings? Why not recover millions in unpaid advertising fees or charge city departments for building maintenance? (Jonker:) “If the City was serious about revenue, it wouldn’t be coming after parks. It would be going after hijacked buildings, collecting what’s owed in advertising revenue, its collected none of that this year! You know they maintain the Joburg city department buildings, they could be billing its own departments for maintenance.” Presenter VO: So come back to the question: why? Presenter Link (on camera, walking through park): We’ve asked a lot of people, some say the City’s budget is under pressure—and instead of fixing its own broken revenue systems, it’s going after the low-hanging fruit: functional parks and sports clubs that already work. With the 2026 local elections approaching, could green spaces be eyed for future low-cost housing? (Presenter VO): On radio, Tshabalala insists that the idea of building housing hasn’t even crossed their minds. Tshabalala Tshabalala on radio interview. “We have not even considered — it has not come to our mind — that there can be potential for a block of flats or residential for that matter. For now, we are looking at the facility in terms of its right, which is looking purely at sports.” (Presenter LINK) [Walking Into Frame – Confront Setup]: Tshabalala says it’s all above board—just about updating old leases. But with the scale of land involved, the laws used, and little transparency, residents are asking: is that really the full story? (Presenter VO): We sat down with Tshabalala to find out. [THE CITY RESPONDS in act 2] LEGALITY & PROCESS You’ve said there’s a notarial lease in place until 2044 for Marks Park—so on what legal basis are you trying to override it now? Isn’t that lease binding? If this is really just a lease review, then why not simply renew the leases? Why invoke the Asset Transfer Regulations—meant for disposing of public land? Why is public participation only happening after Council approval? The law says it must come first—aren’t you in breach of that? TRANSPARENCY & TRUST Why hasn’t the public been told that up to 173 hectares of green space could be affected? At James and Ethel Gray, padel courts popped up with no participation process—and none of that revenue comes back to the City. Why? What participation process was there at Bryanston Sports Club? Posters were hidden. You see, this is why people don’t trust JPC. FINANCIAL LOGIC You’ve claimed Marks Park could generate R10 million in rent. Based on what? Has a feasibility study been done? These clubs already pay for water, electricity, security, and rates—what exactly is the City contributing in return? Wouldn’t it make more financial sense to recover the millions owed by other City departments to JPC for building maintenance—rather than threaten functional green spaces? Why target well-used parks and clubs when hijacked buildings and rundown city properties lie neglected? Why not start there? JPC’S ROLE & OVERREACH Why is the Johannesburg Property Company deciding which sports are “relevant” enough to keep? Isn’t that the mandate of the Sports Department? Where in the City’s business or asset management plan does it say that parks, sports fields, and cemeteries are up for disposal? [FINAL 3 – WHAT’S AT STAKE] (Presenter Link): In principle, most of us agree—land and housing for the poor are essential. But is it any wonder that when proposals like this come from the City, they’re met with deep scepticism? This is the same administration that once promised a “Mega City”… and was later exposed for looting COVID relief funds. Now suddenly, it’s about building homes for the poor? The public’s cynicism isn’t unfounded. Visual: Families in the park. Tai chi in the grass. Soccer games. Laughter. (Presenter VO): If Marks Park falls, what’s next? Melville Koppies? The Botanical Gardens? Jonker: “These spaces aren’t luxuries. They’re constitutional rights. And once they’re gone—we never get them back. You need them to actually put up high rise flats, its part of the city cy-laws to have green spaces” (Presenter link): The City says this is about financial value. But green spaces offer something far more valuable: breathing room, community, connection. (Presenter VO): And before we give that up—we need to ask: who benefits from this? And what will be left for the rest of us? OUTRO – Fade to black. Park aerial fades into city skyline. END. Further information: Visual Note for Script – Director’s Brief We’re aiming for bold, cinematic visuals to anchor this story and give it scale. That means sweeping drone footage of the Johannesburg skyline, contrasted with expansive overhead shots of the green spaces under review—Marks Park, the Botanical Gardens, Melville Koppies, etc. We’ll also need low-angle shots of key city buildings, especially the JPC offices, to visually represent institutional power. Throughout the piece, we’ll cut to “breathing space” moments—scenes of people using the parks. These should feel warm, organic, and grounded: children playing, families relaxing, joggers, dog walkers, informal soccer games. We want the audience to see what's at stake. (We’ll need to get permissions from City Parks to film these areas—potentially with a fee—and I’ll handle those requests.) Framing & Tone: This story has been in the news, so we’re not here to rehash it. We’re here to deepen the conversation and push it forward. That means sharp, informed questioning, paired with a clear and compelling visual narrative. The opening act runs a bit longer—around three minutes—because we need to recap our previous story, introduce the map and the core issue, and establish the key characters driving the narrative. We’ll use Sizakela’s previous public statements (including her radio and Facebook clips) to set up the confrontation efficiently and focus on getting real answers—not soundbites. This is a deliberate decision: keep the confrontation short but meaningful, with layered build-up across the acts. We’ve planted clues throughout the script: In Act 1, we raise early questions about the lease process and hint at the politicking, with political parties calling parks a "luxury." In Act 2, before the confrontation, we introduce deeper suspicions—suggesting these parks may be seen as cash cows or tools to manipulate ward demographics ahead of 2026. Then we go straight into the confrontation—direct, clear, and urgent. Presenter Direction: The presenter must be part of the story. They should be seen walking through the parks, interacting with residents, asking questions aloud, and reacting with genuine curiosity or concern. Their presence anchors the viewer and helps humanise a potentially dry, bureaucratic issue. Tone & Engagement: We’re not doing a long list of case studies—this isn’t a legal brief. We’re taking viewers to Pirates Rugby Club because it’s vibrant and relatable, something our audience will enjoy. We’ll also inject some levity with the AI protest song, and hopefully include community protest visuals if they happen. This is a story about green spaces—but also about power, trust, and the city’s future. So it needs to be sharp, visually rich, and people-focused. Every scene must remind the audience what we’re really fighting to protect. in Show: Title Author Last Updated 10 August 2025 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 17 August 2025 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Shots of other municipalities… and then going into Joburg to widen scope of story… (Moleli VO): Across the country, cash‑strapped municipalities are scrambling to raise money — and Johannesburg seems to have its eye on public spaces - from parks to sports fields. Visual: Drones of these spaces in joburg… (Moleli VO): The City boasts that Joburg is the world’s largest manmade urban forest — but it doesn’t have a formal register of its green spaces. Many are leased to clubs and community groups that maintain and use them. Visual: Close up shots of people using these spaces (Pat Carolin): We are providing a service to the people, now the city is trying to make a decision on what to do with the asset that actually belongs to those people. (Moleli VO): The City has announced the leases of 91 parks and green spaces are being reviewed. And residents fear the real plan is to redevelop or even sell off their beloved parks. (Farouk Khan): We're definitely scared because, obviously, our fate is in the hands of the city council as such. (Moleli VO) Outraged residents are responding as only South Africans can. Visual: protest song clip [TRANSITION] [ACT 1 – THE ALARM IS RAISED] Visual: Cllr Nicolene Jonker at her desk, flipping through the Council agenda. (Moleli VO): Jo’burg councillor Nicolene Jonker was reading through obscure council paperwork when a familiar property caught her eye. (Jonker): To my horror, I saw the name Marks Park. It’s the city’s pride and joy. (Moleli VO): Mark’s Park is a Joburg landmark and home to a range of sports facilities. She’d spotted its name in a report by the Johannesburg Property Company, or JPC, which manages the City’s property portfolio. (Moleli): What made you think something is fishy here? (Jonker): Well, it's speaking about a non-core asset, a non utilised space. And another thing that really stood out was the alienation. (Moleli VO): Oddly, the report described it as a “non‑core asset” and the word “alienation” in property law means there was a planned transfer of ownership through a sale or lease. (Moleli VO): The City’s green space leases typically run for 25 years. Marks Park’s lease was renewed in 2018, and still has 19 years to go. So why announce a review now? According to officials, the property is paying too little. (Tshabalala Facebook video): “If you look at Marks Park, this city is receiving R49 per annum — you can see that doesn’t make any business sense.” (Moleli VO): JPC General Manager Sizeka Tshabalala has told the media the aim is simply to update rentals to match current market values. (Tshabalala): “We anticipate that the rental that we need to get as the city is in excess of R10 million.” (Moleli VO): That’s R10 million for just one property! A substantial jump from what’s currently being paid. The local community believes something much more dubious is behind the move. (Jonker): But this particular item said sale. (Moleli VO): The JPC report appeared to suggest that a 173‑hectare green corridor in the suburb of Emmarentia could be put up for sale. It includes not only Marks Park, but also the Melville Koppies and Botanical Gardens — land donated to the City in the 1930s, on condition it remains public and its biodiversity protected. (show MAP) Moleli: The JPC has suggested sites like Marks Park and various other green spaces could bring in millions for the city? Jonker: I do think it's prime land and they can probably sell it for a lot. But let's be open, honest and tell the residents what you really want to do. (Moleli VO): Carte Blanche and other media have in the past reported on irregular tenders and other allegations linked to senior JPC officials. As a result, public trust in the organisation is low. (Moleli link): The JPC claims it’s cleaning house. But targeting parks and sports grounds to boost revenue, isn’t it driving away the very communities they’re trying to win back? PAUSE (Moleli VO): The parks saga comes amid a significant budget crisis in our economic hub. Simply put, the City is running out of money. In the last financial year, it posted a R300 million deficit, so could it be that the City is now eyeing public assets for revenue? Pat Carolin manages the Bryanston Sport Club and says they're anything but lucrative. (Pat Carolin): We're a municipal non-profit club open to the public, and we run at a small loss of about R150,000. Last financial year, we spent R1.3 million just on the maintenance of these grounds. If we were to pay market-related rentals, we wouldn't then be able to afford the maintenance on their asset. (Moleli VO): The club’s lease was up for review late last year. But, oddly, a report on the matter quietly slipped through council - without Bryanston’s management team knowing. Pause: Mac and Carolin playing Tennis - DRONE and closeup visuals Changing the lease on properties valued above R10 million - like Marks Park and the Bryanston Sports Club - requires public participation. But, by June, Bryanston had missed the opportunity to object. (Pat Carolin): They didn't notify any of the local newspapers. Even the delivery of the notice to us was shrouded in a bit of secrecy. We found it lying on the floor outside. This notice wasn’t dated. Pause: Go to Emmarentia Dam sequence with Mac (Moleli VO): Marks Park and Bryanston Sports Club are among 91 public spaces under review. Each has its own report, with the City looking to charge what the properties are worth. (Moleli link): So, here’s the problem, no one outside of council has actually seen the report. And until it’s made public, no one really knows what it says. (Moleli VO): But we did find evidence for Jonker’s claim that the City plans to sell parks, not JUST renegotiate the leases. It’s in a tender document explicitly listing Marks Park for sale. PAUSE…. [ACT 2 – THE MONEY AND WHO DO YOU TRUST?] (Moleli Link): So, are residents right to be worried about this land — or is it, as the JPC insists, just business as usual? We're here to cut through the noise and hear exactly what the JPC has to say. Drone JPC (Moleli VO): The JPC’s Sizeka Tshabalala says this is all a simple misunderstanding. But, from the outset, appears confused about the very origin of Mark’s Park. (Moleli): Was this land donated to the city? (Tshabalala): No, no it was purchased by the city in and around 1943. (Moleli VO): We asked, but the City didn’t show us the purchase agreement, citing privacy. MAP Tshabalala clarified that the City isn’t reviewing leases on the entire 173 hectare green belt: only Marks Park. NOT the Koppies or Botanical Gardens. She says the current Marks Park lease is invalid because there was no public participation when it was renewed in 2018. (Tshabalala): Before any lease can be concluded, there's always a council approval or a resolution. And there must also be a notice. We don't have a record of that. (Moleli): Can it truly generate up to R10 million in rental? (Tshabalala): I think it can, because when we get evaluation, it is from a professional, so if we are leasing it for 25 years, the valuation report advises us, over that period, you can generate this much. (Moleli): You are not selling this land? (Tshabalala): We are still going to continue leasing it for the same exact usage which is sports and recreation. (Moleli VO): If that’s the case, why does the word “sale” appear on the council report - and on a tender document we uncovered? Visual: Moleli shows her the document with sale on it. (Moleli): So, I've got a document here. “Public participation for proposed sale”. Surely when people see this they will be worried, because this is obviously your document. City of Joburg, Property Company, in terms of the tender that went out. (Tshabalala): Okay. No, no, no. It is not for a sale. (Moleli): So, is this wrong? (Tshabalala): Yes, it’s wrong. We have amended it. (Moleli): When was it amended? (Tshabalala): It has been amended right now. (Moleli VO): But it’s not the first time this “mistake” has happened. The same “sale” slip up was repeated in the documents referring to Bryanston Sports Club. (Tshabalala): We’re issuing an erratum, because it made reference to a sale instead of a lease. (Moleli): Who keeps on making this mistake of a sale? Who writes these tender documents? (Tshabalala): We compile a list of what needs to be done and we appoint service providers. (Moleli): For Marks Park and now for Bryanston you're saying the same mistake was made. (Tshabalala): It’s an erratum, yes. (Moleli VO): But, sale or lease, it’s hard to avoid a glaring irony: The City wants to void the Mark’s Park lease because of a lack of public participation when it was renewed, and yet it apparently failed to conduct a public participation at Bryanston. (Moleli): Were any local papers contacted? (Tshabalala): Right now that's the process that we are following. (Moleli link): So even if we accept that the word ‘sale’ was just a mistake and they meant ‘lease’ ... Either way, the money doesn’t go to the JPC. It goes directly to the city. and given their track record, that’s a concern. [PAUSE] [FINAL ACT 3 – WHAT’S AT STAKE] Visuals of COUNCIL MEETING - Moleli comes to council chambers and watches… (Moleli VO): Tshabalala promised the controversial JPC report would go before council for a vote the following day, but that didn’t happen. (Joburg Councilor): We would like on behalf of the executive to withdraw… item 42 (Moleli link)(no tracksuit): It’s no surprise that after our interview with the JPC, item 42, which was meant to discuss the sale or lease of marks park was suddenly removed from the agenda… (Jonker): It shows me that they've listened. They've listened to you, as Carte Blanche. but it's not off the table. (Moleli VO): The JPC later confirmed it withdrew the report due to “factual” errors. (Jonker:) To write out sale versus lease, it's totally different keys to type. (Moleli link)(no tracksuit): Conversations about land use are important, but can you really blame the public for being little bit sceptical? This is the very department that was exposed for looting covid relief funds, and now they’re saying it's about the public benefiting from green spaces? Come on! END. OUTRO: The city says they withdrew TEASER FOR CAP ON TUESDAY WP_FX3_2062 01:00: A CITY PROPOSAL, THREE SUSPICIOUS TYPING ERRORS AND LAND THAT COULD BE SOLD OR LEASED - ALL IN THE NAME OF PUBLIC BENEFIT, BUT WITH THE CITY’S HISTORY OF MISMANAGEMENT AND BROKEN PROMISES, RESIDENTS ARE NOT BUYING THE OFFICIAL STORY. PROMO 1 X 21 seconds: VO: From botanical gardens to rugby fields… the city says it’s just reviewing leases. But residents fear a land grab is already underway. Upsound: Farouk Khan: We're definitely scared because, obviously, our fate is in the hands of the city council VO: What’s really behind the City’s park review? PROMO 2: “Follow the Money” Jonker: If I didn’t make this big who-ha nobody would have known. Upsound: (Pat Carolin): We are providing a service to the people, now the city is trying to make a decision on what to do with the asset that actually belongs to those people. VO: Is the City targeting public green spaces as a way to cash in? PROMO 3: “Face to Face” (Confrontation Tease) VO: Are public green spaces up for sale or for lease renewal? (Tshabalala) No, no, no. It is not for a sale. (Moleli) Is this wrong? (Tshabalala) We have amended it. VO: Is there more to the City’s park review than meets the eye?

metadata.Unique Selling Point: We are going to take the story forward and not just recap, we are trying to get to the bottom of why by questioning everything. We have an interview secured with Sizakela from JPC.
metadata.Summary: [OPENING ACT – VISUAL INTRO] Visual: Sweeping drone shot over Marks Park—lush fields, joggers, kids on swings, dogs chasing frisbees. Cut to the City of Joburg skyline creeping into frame. (Presenter VO): “Lease rationalisation.” “Non-core assets.” And the word that says it all—“alienation.” They sound like routine municipal processes. But in Johannesburg, they’re being used to describe something far more contentious: a proposal that could see iconic green spaces—our city’s lungs—under threat. Visuals: We need to have a montage here are visuals from the story of coming up – maybe from confront/juxtapose with protest/angry residents (Jonker): “These aren’t just empty plots — they’re vital public spaces the City now wants to dispose of, rezone, and sell off. It’s a land grab.” Visual: Map graphic – highlighting RE/33 Braamfontein 53 IR with overlays of areas like Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Botanical Gardens, Froggy Pond, Westdene Dam. (Presenter VO): What’s at stake? This—173 hectares of public land that includes some of Joburg’s most treasured parks and recreation zones. It’s not “just the sports clubs” as the City claims—it’s an entire green corridor that could change forever. [STORY FRAME – SETTING THE STAKES] (Presenter Link): The City insists it’s just policy. But to residents, it feels like a land grab. And behind the bureaucratic jargon lies a simple question: if this was really just about updating leases — why not just renew them? Why launch an entirely new process that opens the door to rezoning, reclassification, and even permanent disposal? That’s what we set out to uncover. Visual: Insert of JPC’s Sizeka Tshabalala from Facebook, then overlay headlines: "SIU finds Helen Botes guilty", "JPC in HAWKS crosshairs", "Joburg residents in uproar over parks". (Presenter VO): PREVIOUS STORY RECAP The Johannesburg Property Company—tasked with leading this controversial land review—says it’s working to rebuild public trust. But its credibility is in tatters. Last year Carte Blanche reported on how its former CEO, Helen Botes, was found guilty of financial misconduct in a Special Investigating Unit probe into COVID-era cleaning tenders—yet she was kept on. Now, formal charges have been filed, and the HAWKS are investigating a lease deal involving Proton House—an inner-city property allegedly handed to politically connected interests under questionable terms. (Presenter Link): The JPC says it’s cleaning house, but keeping Helen Botes in the fold has raised eyebrows—and so has their strategy to earn back the public’s trust. By targeting parks and sports grounds in a bid to boost revenue, are they not alienating the very communities they’re meant to serve? (Presenter VO): Johannesburg Property Company General Manager, Sizakela Tshabalala, has been everywhere—on radio, in print, online—reassuring residents this isn’t a land grab, but a cleanup. Upsound – Facebook video: “Some people are still paying R2 or R49 a year on leases that were signed more than 30 years ago. It’s not sustainable.” “We’re not taking anything away. We’re just trying to modernise, to make it fair.” (Presenter VO): She insists it’s just about bringing outdated leases in line with today’s market. But residents aren’t convinced. Is this really about revenue—or is there a deeper, politically driven agenda at play? Visual: Park/sports visuals throughout entire piece to illustrate what they’re used for. [ACT 1 – THE ALARM IS RAISED] Visual: Cut to Cllr Nicolene Jonker at her desk, flipping through the Council agenda. (Presenter VO): It was buried in the paperwork. A dry-sounding council item about lease reviews. But when DA councillor Nicolene Jonker looked closer, one phrase jumped off the page: Municipal Asset Transfer Regulations. (Jonker): “This isn’t about updating leases. This is a formal alienation process—the first legal step toward disposal.” Visual: Council document highlighting ATR references. Zoom in on phrases like “alienation,” “surplus land,” and “public participation.” (Presenter VO): And that matters. Because the Asset Transfer References are only triggered when a municipality intends to sell or transfer public land. Not when it's simply renewing a lease. Visual: Community protests. Residents holding placards: “HANDS OFF OUR PARKS!” “MARKS PARK IS OURS!” Visual: Cut to the comedic AI-generated protest song. (Presenter VO): Just bringing up this issue sparks outrage in the community. It’s struck such a nerve, even the protests have gone musical. A viral AI-generated anthem did what formal petitions couldn’t—put Joburg on notice. So let’s take a look at the land in question. Visuals: MAP again (Presenter VO): The area flagged in JPC’s own documents spans up to 173 hectares—a sweeping green belt that includes Pirates Club, Marks Park, Emmarentia Dam, Melville Koppies, and parts of the Botanical Gardens. Land is a sensitive subject, but also a political bargaining chip. Now, political parties are jumping on the bandwagon—framing green spaces as a luxury. Some argue these areas could be better used for low-cost housing, rather than recreation. In a city like Johannesburg, green spaces aren’t luxuries—they’re lifelines. Parks and sports grounds are protected public assets, meant to serve communities, not be quietly sold off. (Jonker): The leases could be undervalued, but currently its normal for them to be only R500 a month, not millions. And the current lease holders take care of the properties paying the water/elec/lights, mowing the lawns, so they have value. (Presenter VO): In interviews Tshabalala has said these properties like Marks Park could be worth R10 million. 00:04:00–00:04:22 “So if you look at Marks Park and the fact that when we enter into a lease … considering the value of that property … the lease, if we are looking at its market value today, we anticipate that the rental that we need to get as the city is in excess of R10 million.” (Presenter VO): But could they know that if there’s been no feasibility study done? (Jonker): They’re doing this backwards, you first do the feasibility study, then you do the public participation process, and you give more information about the land. Currently we know nothing. (Presenter VO): And what Sizeka doesn’t say—is that the lease for Marks Park is a notarial one, registered in 1994, valid until 2043. Legally binding. And already limited to sport and recreation. [Examples of where JPC has failed] (Presenter VO): And why should residents trust the Johannesburg Property Company? Its track record is riddled with poor management. Just look at James and Ethel Gray Park—where paddle courts appeared overnight. Jonker (upsound): “Why would you allow these to pop up—and then have no benefit to the City?” (Presenter VO): Was it simple oversight that none of that revenue goes back to the City? And what about Bryanston Sports Club—did residents somehow miss the public participation signs? Jonker (upsound): “They were stuck at the back of the room, facing the wall. No one saw them. Public participation feels like a box-ticking exercise.” (Presenter VO): Now, that sports club is under review. Its future? Completely up to the City. And that’s exactly what’s raising concern. CASE STUDY: PIRATES RUGBY CLUB Cut to: Pirates Rugby Club, where the local manager describes years of community investment, public use, and rising anxiety. Pirates owner: “We run this space for the people. We pay for water, electricity, maintenance—and we’re the ones being targeted?” Visuals: Maybe some humour with presenter – take a breather park visuals. (Presenter VO): On 702 radio, Sizeka Tshabalala says the review isn’t about selling parks, but about unlocking more sports and community opportunities. (approx. 8:52–10:49): “We’re simply looking at how to diversify usage — can we introduce additional sports codes, make these facilities more active and community-focused?” ... We are saying that if there are football grounds, what other sports can we bring into that facility to make it more active?” (Presenter VO): But is that really the job of a property management company? Shouldn’t they be managing assets—not deciding what sports should be played? And if this is really about revenue, why aren’t they looking for money elsewhere? Pause visuals… [ACT 2 – THE MONEY AND WHO DO YOU TRUST?] Visual: Split-screen — on one side, JPC statements. On the other, maps showing affected areas—up to 173 hectares. Cut to aerials of Melville Koppies and Emmarentia Dam. (Presenter VO): And yet, nowhere in the JPC’s own business plan is “disposal of public green space” mentioned. (show business plan visuals) Graphic: City-owned derelict buildings. Hijacked inner-city properties. Overlay: “Why not start here?” (Presenter VO): If the City really wanted to boost revenue, why not start with hijacked buildings? Why not recover millions in unpaid advertising fees or charge city departments for building maintenance? (Jonker:) “If the City was serious about revenue, it wouldn’t be coming after parks. It would be going after hijacked buildings, collecting what’s owed in advertising revenue, its collected none of that this year! You know they maintain the Joburg city department buildings, they could be billing its own departments for maintenance.” Presenter VO: So come back to the question: why? Presenter Link (on camera, walking through park): We’ve asked a lot of people, some say the City’s budget is under pressure—and instead of fixing its own broken revenue systems, it’s going after the low-hanging fruit: functional parks and sports clubs that already work. With the 2026 local elections approaching, could green spaces be eyed for future low-cost housing? (Presenter VO): On radio, Tshabalala insists that the idea of building housing hasn’t even crossed their minds. Tshabalala Tshabalala on radio interview. “We have not even considered — it has not come to our mind — that there can be potential for a block of flats or residential for that matter. For now, we are looking at the facility in terms of its right, which is looking purely at sports.” (Presenter LINK) [Walking Into Frame – Confront Setup]: Tshabalala says it’s all above board—just about updating old leases. But with the scale of land involved, the laws used, and little transparency, residents are asking: is that really the full story? (Presenter VO): We sat down with Tshabalala to find out. [THE CITY RESPONDS in act 2] LEGALITY & PROCESS You’ve said there’s a notarial lease in place until 2044 for Marks Park—so on what legal basis are you trying to override it now? Isn’t that lease binding? If this is really just a lease review, then why not simply renew the leases? Why invoke the Asset Transfer Regulations—meant for disposing of public land? Why is public participation only happening after Council approval? The law says it must come first—aren’t you in breach of that? TRANSPARENCY & TRUST Why hasn’t the public been told that up to 173 hectares of green space could be affected? At James and Ethel Gray, padel courts popped up with no participation process—and none of that revenue comes back to the City. Why? What participation process was there at Bryanston Sports Club? Posters were hidden. You see, this is why people don’t trust JPC. FINANCIAL LOGIC You’ve claimed Marks Park could generate R10 million in rent. Based on what? Has a feasibility study been done? These clubs already pay for water, electricity, security, and rates—what exactly is the City contributing in return? Wouldn’t it make more financial sense to recover the millions owed by other City departments to JPC for building maintenance—rather than threaten functional green spaces? Why target well-used parks and clubs when hijacked buildings and rundown city properties lie neglected? Why not start there? JPC’S ROLE & OVERREACH Why is the Johannesburg Property Company deciding which sports are “relevant” enough to keep? Isn’t that the mandate of the Sports Department? Where in the City’s business or asset management plan does it say that parks, sports fields, and cemeteries are up for disposal? [FINAL 3 – WHAT’S AT STAKE] (Presenter Link): In principle, most of us agree—land and housing for the poor are essential. But is it any wonder that when proposals like this come from the City, they’re met with deep scepticism? This is the same administration that once promised a “Mega City”… and was later exposed for looting COVID relief funds. Now suddenly, it’s about building homes for the poor? The public’s cynicism isn’t unfounded. Visual: Families in the park. Tai chi in the grass. Soccer games. Laughter. (Presenter VO): If Marks Park falls, what’s next? Melville Koppies? The Botanical Gardens? Jonker: “These spaces aren’t luxuries. They’re constitutional rights. And once they’re gone—we never get them back. You need them to actually put up high rise flats, its part of the city cy-laws to have green spaces” (Presenter link): The City says this is about financial value. But green spaces offer something far more valuable: breathing room, community, connection. (Presenter VO): And before we give that up—we need to ask: who benefits from this? And what will be left for the rest of us? OUTRO – Fade to black. Park aerial fades into city skyline. END.
metadata.Further information: Visual Note for Script – Director’s Brief We’re aiming for bold, cinematic visuals to anchor this story and give it scale. That means sweeping drone footage of the Johannesburg skyline, contrasted with expansive overhead shots of the green spaces under review—Marks Park, the Botanical Gardens, Melville Koppies, etc. We’ll also need low-angle shots of key city buildings, especially the JPC offices, to visually represent institutional power. Throughout the piece, we’ll cut to “breathing space” moments—scenes of people using the parks. These should feel warm, organic, and grounded: children playing, families relaxing, joggers, dog walkers, informal soccer games. We want the audience to see what's at stake. (We’ll need to get permissions from City Parks to film these areas—potentially with a fee—and I’ll handle those requests.) Framing & Tone: This story has been in the news, so we’re not here to rehash it. We’re here to deepen the conversation and push it forward. That means sharp, informed questioning, paired with a clear and compelling visual narrative. The opening act runs a bit longer—around three minutes—because we need to recap our previous story, introduce the map and the core issue, and establish the key characters driving the narrative. We’ll use Sizakela’s previous public statements (including her radio and Facebook clips) to set up the confrontation efficiently and focus on getting real answers—not soundbites. This is a deliberate decision: keep the confrontation short but meaningful, with layered build-up across the acts. We’ve planted clues throughout the script: In Act 1, we raise early questions about the lease process and hint at the politicking, with political parties calling parks a "luxury." In Act 2, before the confrontation, we introduce deeper suspicions—suggesting these parks may be seen as cash cows or tools to manipulate ward demographics ahead of 2026. Then we go straight into the confrontation—direct, clear, and urgent. Presenter Direction: The presenter must be part of the story. They should be seen walking through the parks, interacting with residents, asking questions aloud, and reacting with genuine curiosity or concern. Their presence anchors the viewer and helps humanise a potentially dry, bureaucratic issue. Tone & Engagement: We’re not doing a long list of case studies—this isn’t a legal brief. We’re taking viewers to Pirates Rugby Club because it’s vibrant and relatable, something our audience will enjoy. We’ll also inject some levity with the AI protest song, and hopefully include community protest visuals if they happen. This is a story about green spaces—but also about power, trust, and the city’s future. So it needs to be sharp, visually rich, and people-focused. Every scene must remind the audience what we’re really fighting to protect.
